blocks.title: Northwind's footprint: sources feeding one inventory

scenes.caption: Each public source answers a different question about the same organisation.
Registration, DNS and certificate logs give names and providers: what exists.
Search engines, code hosts and job adverts give context: what leaks and what technology is in use.
The inventory is compared with what the organisation thinks it has. Differences become findings with owners.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**

- **Prevent**: one owner and an expiry alert for every domain (a lapsed domain can be registered by someone else, along with the email and trust that pointed at it); a review step for what job adverts and press releases say about internal tools; secret scanning on code hosts.
- **Detect**: run the inventory on a schedule and diff it. A new hostname in CT logs that nobody ordered, or a new public repository, is a signal to investigate.
- **Respond**: give each finding an owner and a deadline. Anything secret that was public is treated as compromised and rotated, not just deleted.

blocks.prompt: Northwind's RDAP record shows the main domain expires in 40 days and auto-renew is off. Is that a security finding or an admin chore?
blocks.reveal: **A security finding.** If the domain lapses, its website and email stop working, and someone else may be able to register it. Whoever does then receives email sent to the old addresses (including password resets) and can host pages that customers trust. Give it an owner, renew it, and turn on auto-renew and registrar locks.

blocks.md: Point OSINT at yourself first. Registration data, DNS, certificate logs, search engines, code hosts and job adverts together describe what an attacker sees; an inventory diffed on a schedule turns that into findings.

blocks.question: Why is RDAP easier to automate than the old WHOIS?
options: It requires no internet connection
It shows registrants' home addresses
Queries are HTTPS addresses and replies are structured JSON
It only works for .com domains
blocks.explain: RFC 9082 defines queries as HTTP URLs and RFC 9083 defines JSON responses, so a script can parse fields reliably. Personal data is usually redacted, and RDAP serves many top-level domains (TLDs, such as .com or .org).

blocks.question: A CT log shows a new certificate for `payroll-old.northwind.example` that no team requested. What should the security team do first?
options: Ignore it: certificates are public anyway
Treat it as a finding: find who requested it and whether the host should exist
Delete the CT log entry
Publish the hostname on social media to warn others
blocks.explain: An unexpected certificate means an unmanaged system or a mis-issuing certificate authority. CT logs are append-only, so the entry cannot be deleted; the response is to find the owner.

lessons.title: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves

blocks.md:
**Metadata** is data about data. The Berkeley Protocol lists typical examples: "the creator of a file, its date of creation, upload data, modifications, file size and geodata." Files carry it silently, and whoever downloads the file gets it too.

Tiny example: a staff member photographs the new office kitchen for the company blog. The JPEG file records the camera model, the exact time, and the GPS position of the phone. The blog post is harmless; the file may not be.

Photos use **Exif** (Exchangeable image file format), a standard maintained by CIPA (the Camera & Imaging Products Association, the Japanese camera industry body) together with JEITA (the Japan Electronics and Information Technology Industries Association). The current edition is Exif 3.1 (CIPA DC-008, January 2026).

Inside a JPEG, Exif data sits in tagged directories called IFDs (image file directories): a main one (camera make and model), an Exif IFD (such as `DateTimeOriginal`, when the picture was taken) and a GPS IFD. Latitude and longitude are stored as three numbers (degrees, minutes, seconds) plus a reference letter: N or S, E or W.

Documents carry metadata too: office files record an author and last editor, and PDFs record the software that produced them.

blocks.code:
from PIL import Image
from PIL.ExifTags import Base, GPS, IFD

# A test photo with made-up metadata (a public landmark, no person)
img = Image.new("RGB", (64, 48), "gray")
exif = Image.Exif()
exif[Base.Make], exif[Base.Model] = "ExampleCam", "X100"
exif.get_ifd(IFD.Exif)[Base.DateTimeOriginal] = "2025:06:21 14:05:09"
gps = exif.get_ifd(IFD.GPSInfo)
gps[GPS.GPSLatitudeRef], gps[GPS.GPSLatitude] = "N", (48.0, 51.0, 30.24)
gps[GPS.GPSLongitudeRef], gps[GPS.GPSLongitude] = "E", (2.0, 17.0, 40.2)
img.save("photo.jpg", exif=exif)

def to_decimal(dms, ref):
    d, m, s = (float(x) for x in dms)
    value = d + m / 60 + s / 3600
    return -value if ref in ("S", "W") else value

# Read it back, as anyone who downloads the file can
e = Image.open("photo.jpg").getexif()
g = e.get_ifd(IFD.GPSInfo)
print("Camera:", e[Base.Make], e[Base.Model])
print("Taken: ", e.get_ifd(IFD.Exif)[Base.DateTimeOriginal])
lat = to_decimal(g[GPS.GPSLatitude], g[GPS.GPSLatitudeRef])
lon = to_decimal(g[GPS.GPSLongitude], g[GPS.GPSLongitudeRef])
print(f"GPS:    {lat:.5f}, {lon:.5f}")

# Strip it, as a publisher should: re-save with empty Exif
Image.open("photo.jpg").save("clean.jpg", exif=b"")
print("After strip:", dict(Image.open("clean.jpg").getexif()))
blocks.caption: Runs with Pillow (a Python imaging library). The test photo is made up; the coordinates are the Eiffel Tower.

blocks.code:
Camera: ExampleCam X100
Taken:  2025:06:21 14:05:09
GPS:    48.85840, 2.29450
After strip: {}
blocks.caption: Real output. Anyone who downloads photo.jpg reads the same three lines; clean.jpg carries no Exif at all.

blocks.title: Turning stored degrees, minutes, seconds into a map position

scenes.caption: The GPS IFD stores latitude as three numbers: 48 degrees, 51 minutes, 30.24 seconds, with reference N.
A minute is 1/60 of a degree and a second 1/3600, so each part is divided by its unit.
48 + 0.85 + 0.0084 = 48.8584 degrees north. Longitude works the same way: 2 + 17/60 + 40.2/3600 = 2.2945 east. S or W would make the value negative.

blocks.md:
**Using metadata as an investigator.** Metadata can support or undermine a claim, but it is easily edited and often missing. The Berkeley Protocol warns that platforms "often transcode uploaded media", so the metadata you see may describe the platform's re-encoded copy, not the original. Treat it as one clue to be corroborated, never as proof on its own.

**Case: Parler, January 2021.** When the Parler social network's public posts were archived in bulk (lesson 13), Gizmodo reported that the site "had no mechanism in place to strip sensitive metadata" from uploaded videos, and used GPS coordinates from 618 Parler videos to place hundreds of them near the US Capitol during the riot of 6 January 2021. A platform's failure to strip metadata turned ordinary uploads into location records. The 2018 leak through the heatmap of Strava (a fitness-tracking app) that showed users' activity, covered in *Privacy engineering*, is the aggregate version of the same lesson.

**Defender view.**

- **Prevent**: strip metadata in the publishing workflow (website uploads, press kits, document exports), using an allowlist of fields to keep rather than a list of fields to remove. Turn off location tagging on work phones' cameras where it is not needed.
- **Detect**: periodically download your own published files and check them for GPS tags, author names and internal paths.
- **Respond**: replace the file, then remember that copies and caches may persist; assume the data was seen.

Stripping Exif is not the only step. Other containers (XMP, Adobe's Extensible Metadata Platform; IPTC fields, from the International Press Telecommunications Council's photo metadata standard; document properties) and the picture itself (a street sign, a view from a window) can reveal location. Look at what the image shows, not only its tags.
Files describe themselves. Read metadata as one clue that needs corroboration; remove it from everything you publish.

blocks.question: A video downloaded from a social platform has a creation date one day after the event it claims to show. What is the best conclusion?
options: The metadata may describe the platform's re-encoded copy; corroborate the date by other means
The video is fake
The event happened a day later than reported
Metadata is always accurate, so the uploader lied
blocks.explain: The Berkeley Protocol notes that platforms transcode uploads, so metadata may reflect the new file, not the original. A date mismatch is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

blocks.question: Which publishing control best prevents GPS leaks from staff photos on the company website?
options: Asking staff to be careful
Removing only the GPSLatitude tag
Blurring faces
Re-encoding uploads and keeping only an allowlist of safe fields
blocks.explain: An allowlist removes everything not explicitly needed, including tags nobody thought of. Removing one tag leaves longitude and other location fields; blurring faces does nothing for metadata.

lessons.title: Verifying images and claims: provenance, reposts and hashes

blocks.md:
Most false images online are not clever fakes. They are real pictures from another time or place, reposted with a new caption. Verification starts by asking where an image came from and when it first appeared.

Tiny example: a photo of a flooded street goes viral with the caption "this morning in our city". A reverse image search finds the same photo in a news article from four years earlier, in another country. The picture is real; the claim is false. This is what the Berkeley Protocol calls **decontextualisation**.

**The Berkeley Protocol's three angles on any item**:

- **Source analysis**: who posted it, and is that consistent with their history? Find the **provenance**, the earliest known appearance. The Protocol advises saying "first copy found online" rather than "the first copy online", since the original may have been deleted or shared privately first.
- **Technical analysis**: the file itself, including metadata (lesson 7) and signs of editing.
- **Content analysis**: what the picture shows, checked against "objectively verifiable information" such as the weather that day or the location of a building, plus geolocation (lesson 9) and chronolocation (lesson 10).

It also warns about **circular reporting**: five articles that all cite one unverified post are one source, not five.

**How a search engine finds "the same picture".** Cryptographic hashes such as SHA-256 change completely if one pixel changes, so they cannot match a resized repost. **Perceptual hashes** summarise what the picture looks like instead. Neal Krawetz, a forensics researcher, described a simple one called **dHash** (difference hash) on the Hacker Factor blog in 2013: convert to grayscale, shrink to 9x8 pixels, then for each row record whether each pixel is brighter than its right-hand neighbour. Eight comparisons per row times eight rows gives 64 bits.

Two images are compared by **Hamming distance**, the number of bits that differ. Krawetz's thresholds: 0 means the same hash and likely a similar picture, 1 to 10 potentially a variation, over 10 likely a different image.

blocks.title: dHash on a 9x8 thumbnail of a made-up skyline

scenes.caption: The image shrunk to 9 columns by 8 rows of brightness values (0 black, 255 white). Dark buildings stand against a light sky.
Row 2: 214 > 222? no (0). 222 > 110? yes (1). 110 > 140? no (0). Each pair of neighbours gives one bit; this row hashes to 01001100.

A repost that is smaller and brighter: almost every value rose by 25 (a few bright cells hit the 255 cap or shifted in resampling). Every comparison between neighbours comes out the same, so all 64 bits match: distance 0.

blocks.code:
from PIL import Image

def dhash(img):
    # Krawetz's dHash: grayscale, shrink to 9x8, compare neighbours
    small = img.convert("L").resize((9, 8), Image.Resampling.LANCZOS)
    px = list(small.get_flattened_data())
    bits = ""
    for row in range(8):
        for col in range(8):
            left, right = px[row * 9 + col], px[row * 9 + col + 1]
            bits += "1" if left > right else "0"
    return bits                                   # 64 bits

def hamming(a, b):
    return sum(x != y for x, y in zip(a, b))      # bits that differ

# orig: a made-up skyline image, 360x320 pixels
repost  = orig.resize((180, 160)).convert("L").point(lambda v: min(255, v + 25))
cropped = orig.crop((60, 0, 360, 320))
flipped = orig.transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)
# Output:
# repost (smaller, brighter)  distance  0 / 64
# cropped                     distance 21 / 64
# mirrored                    distance 24 / 64
blocks.caption: Condensed from a script run with Pillow; output is real. Resizing and brightening do not change the hash; cropping and mirroring do.

blocks.title: Hamming distance from the original (64 bits)

scenes.caption: Resized and brightened: distance 0. dHash survives the changes reposting usually makes.

blocks.prompt: A disinformation account mirrors an old photo left to right and crops it before reposting. Will a dHash-style lookup still find the original?
blocks.reveal: **Probably not.** In the run above, cropping gave distance 21 and mirroring 24, both well past Krawetz's threshold of 10. Real reverse image search engines use more robust features than dHash, but crops and mirrors are still a known way to slip past matching. So try mirroring the image yourself before searching, search distinctive crops, and use more than one engine.

blocks.md: **Content Credentials.** The C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) specification lets cameras and editing tools attach a signed **manifest** to a file: **assertions** about how it was made and edited, bound to the content by cryptographic hashes and signed by the tool. A validator can confirm that the manifest is intact and matches the content. The specification states it should not provide value judgements about whether provenance data is "good" or "bad": a valid manifest says who signed what, not that the scene is true. A missing manifest proves nothing either, since most images have none and stripping is easy.
Ask where and when an image first appeared before asking whether it was edited. Perceptual hashes find reposts; provenance and corroboration decide the claim.

blocks.question: Two news articles and three social posts all report the same event, each linking back to one anonymous video. How many independent sources do you have?
options: Five
One
Three
None, since anonymous videos cannot be used
blocks.explain: That is circular reporting: everything traces back to one video. Anonymous material can still be verified on its content, so it is one source to verify, not none and not five.

blocks.question: Why can a SHA-256 hash not find a resized repost of a photo, while dHash can?
options: SHA-256 is too slow for images
dHash uses a secret key
SHA-256 changes completely when any byte changes; dHash compares brightness patterns that resizing keeps
SHA-256 only works on text
blocks.explain: Cryptographic hashes are designed so any change gives an unrelated hash. dHash records which neighbour is brighter, a pattern that survives resizing and uniform brightness changes.

lessons.title: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken

blocks.md:
**Geolocation**, in the Berkeley Protocol's words, is "the identification or estimation of the location of an object, an activity or the location from which an item was generated", for example by "identifying unique geographic features in a photograph with their actual location on a map". It is how investigators test claims like "this video shows an attack in town X".

Tiny example: a video claims to show a protest outside a city's town hall. The town hall has a clock tower with four windows; the video shows a tower with three. Before any other analysis, the claim is in doubt.

**The method** follows a guide Eliot Higgins, the founder of Bellingcat, published in 2014 on geolocating videos from Libya:

1. **List clues** in the image: landmarks (a minaret, a tower), road features (a central median, lane widths, curves, junctions), building types and heights, vegetation, signs and their language.
2. **Bound the area** using the claim and context: which town, which district.
3. **Search satellite imagery** of that area for the most distinctive clue first. Higgins used a mosque's minaret and dome, then checked the road's curve and the trees opposite.
4. **Eliminate candidates** clue by clue until one place fits everything.
5. **Confirm with something independent**: another feature that appears at the right position, such as an open area at the right point in the video.

The Protocol calls this **spatial analysis** and asks that features be checked "at an appropriate resolution" against satellite images and maps.

blocks.title: Eliminating candidate junctions clue by clue (fictional town)
blocks.code:
# Clues read from a (fictional) street video, each a yes/no test
clues = {
    "road has a central median": lambda c: c["median"],
    "tower visible on the left":  lambda c: c["tower_side"] == "left",
    "road bends right after it":  lambda c: c["bend"] == "right",
    "single-storey buildings":    lambda c: c["storeys"] == 1,
}
# Candidate junctions noted from satellite imagery of the area
candidates = [
    dict(id="J1", median=True,  tower_side="left",  bend="right", storeys=2),
    dict(id="J2", median=False, tower_side="left",  bend="right", storeys=1),
    dict(id="J3", median=True,  tower_side="right", bend="right", storeys=1),
    dict(id="J4", median=True,  tower_side="left",  bend="right", storeys=1),
    dict(id="J5", median=True,  tower_side="left",  bend="left",  storeys=1),
    dict(id="J6", median=True,  tower_side=None,    bend="right", storeys=1),
]
left = candidates
for clue, test in clues.items():
    left = [c for c in left if test(c)]
    print(f"{clue:28s} left: {[c['id'] for c in left]}")

scenes.caption: Six junctions in the claimed area were noted from satellite imagery. The video shows four clues; each becomes a yes or no test.
A central median rules out J2.
scenes.output: road has a central median    left: ['J1', 'J3', 'J4', 'J5', 'J6']

scenes.caption: The tower must be on the left: J3 has it on the right, J6 has none.
scenes.output: tower visible on the left    left: ['J1', 'J4', 'J5']

scenes.caption: The road bends right after the tower: J5 bends left.
scenes.output: road bends right after it    left: ['J1', 'J4']

scenes.caption: Single-storey buildings rule out J1. One candidate fits every clue; it still needs an independent confirming feature before it counts as geolocated.

blocks.title: The same elimination as a grid of candidates

scenes.caption: Six candidates, all possible at the start.
After the median and tower clues: J2, J3 and J6 are out.
After the bend and building clues: only J4 remains. Order matters for effort, not for the answer: start with the clue that cuts the most.

blocks.md: Geolocate places and events, not private people. Working out where a private individual lives or goes from their photos is stalking, whatever the technique is called. Practise on public landmarks, games built for it, or published case studies.

**Failure modes.**

- **Confirmation bias**: deciding on the answer and then seeing matching features. The Berkeley Protocol's objectivity principle asks for multiple working hypotheses; actively look for features that would *disprove* your match.
- **Old imagery**: satellite and street-level pictures may predate construction or demolition. Note the imagery date.
- **Generic features**: a median strip and a minaret describe thousands of junctions. A match needs a combination nothing else in the area has.

**Defender view.** The same method works against your organisation: photos of a secure site's interior, a badge on a lanyard, or a window view can place a sensitive facility. Review photos before publication for what they show, not only their metadata.
List clues, bound the area, eliminate candidates with the most distinctive clue first, then confirm with an independent feature. Report what matched and what could not be checked.

blocks.question: Your best match fits three of four clues, but a building visible in the video is missing from the satellite image. What is the right next step?
options: Declare the match, since three of four is strong
Discard the candidate immediately
Ignore the building as noise
Check the imagery date; if the building is newer than the imagery, look for more recent imagery to confirm
blocks.explain: Imagery age is a known failure mode. A missing building can mean the wrong place or old imagery; resolve which before deciding. Declaring or discarding without checking are both premature.

blocks.question: Why look for features that would disprove your candidate location?
options: To counter confirmation bias, as the Berkeley Protocol's objectivity principle asks
Because courts require exactly ten features
To make the investigation take longer
Because satellite images are always wrong
blocks.explain: Investigators tend to see what they expect. Testing for disconfirming evidence and keeping multiple hypotheses is the Protocol's countermeasure.

lessons.title: Chronolocation: telling the time from shadows

blocks.md:
**Chronolocation** is "the corroboration of the dates and times of the events depicted", for example by "examining the length of the shadows made by sunlight" (Berkeley Protocol). Shadows are a clock anyone can read, because the sun's position at a known place and date can be calculated exactly.

Tiny example: a photo claims to show a rally at 9 in the morning in Paris in June. The shadows are short and point roughly north. In Paris in June the sun is in the east at 9, so shadows point west and are long. Something is wrong with the claim.

**The geometry.** The sun's position is two angles. **Elevation** is its height above the horizon; **azimuth** is its compass direction, measured clockwise from north (90 east, 180 south, 270 west). For an upright object of height $h$ on flat ground, the shadow length $s$ depends only on elevation, and the shadow points directly away from the sun:

blocks.caption: Flat ground and an upright object assumed. Slopes and leaning objects need correction.

blocks.md: The sun's angles for any place and time come from published astronomy equations. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) documents the ones behind its solar calculator, "based on equations from Astronomical Algorithms, by Jean Meeus". The script below uses them for the Eiffel Tower on the summer solstice, 21 June 2025, with no correction for atmospheric refraction (a small effect except near the horizon). An independent library, astral, gave the same angles to one decimal place.

blocks.code:
import math
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
from noaa_sun import sun_position    # NOAA solar calculator equations (Meeus)

LAT, LON = 48.8584, 2.2945           # Eiffel Tower, Paris
CEST = timezone(timedelta(hours=2))  # Paris summer time, UTC+2
for hh in range(8, 21, 2):
    t = datetime(2025, 6, 21, hh, tzinfo=CEST).astimezone(timezone.utc)
    el, az = sun_position(t, LAT, LON)
    ratio = 1 / math.tan(math.radians(el))   # shadow length / height
    print(f"{hh:02d}:00  elev {el:4.1f}  azimuth {az:5.1f}  shadow/height {ratio:.2f}")

# Output:
# 08:00  elev 18.6  azimuth  75.4  shadow/height 2.97
# 10:00  elev 38.2  azimuth  97.5  shadow/height 1.27
# 12:00  elev 56.3  azimuth 128.7  shadow/height 0.67
# 14:00  elev 64.5  azimuth 183.9  shadow/height 0.48
# 16:00  elev 54.3  azimuth 236.1  shadow/height 0.72
# 18:00  elev 35.8  azimuth 265.4  shadow/height 1.39
# 20:00  elev 16.3  azimuth 287.2  shadow/height 3.42
blocks.caption: noaa_sun.sun_position implements the equations on NOAA's calculation-details page (about 35 lines, omitted here). Times are Paris summer time.

blocks.title: Shadow length per metre of height, against sun elevation

scenes.caption: Low sun, long shadows: at 18.6 degrees (08:00) a 1 m post casts a 2.97 m shadow.
At the day's highest point, about 64.6 degrees at 13:53, the ratio bottoms out near 0.48. In Paris it never gets shorter in 2025.
A measured ratio of 0.72 needs an elevation of about 54 degrees. The sun passes 54 degrees twice: once before noon and once after.

blocks.md:
**Worked example (fictional photo).** A photo said to be from the Champ de Mars on 21 June 2025 shows a 1.8 m lamp post with a 1.3 m shadow pointing roughly northeast.

- Ratio: $1.3 / 1.8 = 0.72$, so elevation is about 54.2 degrees.
- Searching the day minute by minute, the sun reaches that elevation at **11:44** (sun azimuth 123.5, shadow pointing 303.5, northwest) and at **16:01** (sun azimuth 236.4, shadow pointing 56.4, northeast).
- The shadow points northeast, so the photo fits about 16:00, not late morning. Allowing 0.05 of error in the ratio gives a window of 15:47 to 16:14.

Length alone gave two answers; direction picked one. A caption claiming "midday" would not fit.

blocks.title: Sun elevation at the Eiffel Tower, 21 June 2025 (degrees)

scenes.caption: Elevation rises and falls through the day, peaking near 13:53 local time (solar noon falls late on the clock because Paris keeps UTC+2 in summer while lying about 2 degrees east of Greenwich).
The two moments near 54 degrees: just before 12:00 and just after 16:00. Only the afternoon one has shadows pointing northeast.

blocks.md:
**Limits.** You need the right date and place first (geolocation comes before chronolocation), an object you can assume is vertical, a known or estimated height, and flat ground. Lens distortion and perspective change apparent lengths, so investigators measure against objects in the same plane or use satellite imagery to find true directions. Report a time *window*, not a minute.

Bellingcat used exactly this reasoning in its 2014 MH17 report: shadows in a photo from Torez put the time at approximately 12:30, which matched timestamped posts reporting a convoy at 12:07, 12:15 and 12:26 (lesson 11).
Shadow length gives the sun's elevation, shadow direction gives its azimuth, and an astronomical calculation turns both into a time window for a known place and date.

blocks.question: A 2 m sign casts a 2 m shadow. What is the sun's elevation?
options: 90 degrees
30 degrees
45 degrees
60 degrees
blocks.explain: s/h = 1 means tan(elevation) = 1, so elevation is 45 degrees. Higher sun would give a shorter shadow; 30 degrees would give a ratio of about 1.73.

blocks.question: Shadow length matches two times of day. What resolves which one?
options: The colour of the sky
The shadow's direction, which follows the sun's azimuth
The photo's file size
Nothing; it can never be resolved
blocks.explain: Before noon the sun is in the east and shadows point west; after noon the reverse. Direction separates the two times that share an elevation.

lessons.title: Case: MH17 and the open-source trail of a missile launcher

blocks.md:
On 17 July 2014 Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 was shot down over eastern Ukraine; all 283 passengers and 15 crew, 298 people, were killed. Within hours, photos and videos of a Buk surface-to-air missile launcher (official reports call the self-propelled launcher vehicle a TELAR, short for transporter erector launcher and radar) moving through the region appeared on social media. This lesson follows how open-source investigators, led by Bellingcat, used the methods of lessons 7 to 10 on that public material, and how their findings later compared with official investigators and a court.

It is a public case about a military vehicle, not about private individuals, which is why it is a model for this course.

**What Bellingcat's November 2014 report did** (*Origin of the Separatists' Buk*):

- **Collected** photos and videos posted on VKontakte and Odnoklassniki (Russian social networks), YouTube, Twitter and Instagram, plus press photos.
- **Geolocated** each one: a photo from the French weekly Paris Match to a motorway in Donetsk, a photo in Torez to its exact spot, a Snizhne photo to a street address less than 1 km from a video of the same vehicle, and a video from Luhansk by matching a billboard, contradicting a Russian Defence Ministry claim about the place.
- **Chronolocated** them: shadows in the Donetsk photo were consistent with the publisher's "about 11 am"; shadows in Torez indicated about 12:30, matching timestamped posts at 12:07, 12:15 and 12:26; Snizhne shadows indicated about 1:30 pm.
- **Identified the vehicle** by a "fingerprint" of markings and damage to its side skirts, compared with 16 videos of a convoy moving from Kursk in Russia on 23 to 25 June 2014, linking it to a launcher numbered 3x2 (its middle digit worn off) of Russia's 53rd Anti-Aircraft Missile Brigade.

blocks.title: The launcher's route on 17 and 18 July 2014, as geolocated

scenes.caption: Morning, 17 July: a photo places the launcher on a low-loader in Donetsk, heading east. Shadows fit the stated time of about 11:00.
Torez, about 12:30 by shadows, matching three timestamped posts about a convoy. Snizhne, about 13:30 by shadows: unloaded and driving south.
The missile was fired from a field south of Snizhne; the court later placed it at a farm field near Pervomaiskyi.
Morning, 18 July: a video filmed in Luhansk, geolocated by a billboard, shows the launcher travelling east.

blocks.code:
# Sightings on 17 July 2014 as reported by Bellingcat (Nov 2014), local
# time, with what fixed each time.
sightings = [
    ("Donetsk", "11:00", "publisher's stated time"),
    ("Torez",   "12:07", "timestamped posts"),
    ("Torez",   "12:15", "timestamped posts"),
    ("Torez",   "12:26", "timestamped posts"),
    ("Torez",   "12:30", "shadows"),
    ("Snizhne", "13:30", "shadows"),
]
route = ["Donetsk", "Torez", "Snizhne"]          # in order along the road

def minutes(hhmm):
    h, m = hhmm.split(":")
    return int(h) * 60 + int(m)

ok = True
for (p1, t1, _), (p2, t2, _) in zip(sightings, sightings[1:]):
    if minutes(t2) < minutes(t1) or route.index(p2) < route.index(p1):
        ok = False
        print("conflict:", p1, t1, "then", p2, t2)
print("kinds of timing evidence:", sorted({s[2] for s in sightings}))
print("consistent with one trip along the road:", ok)

# Output:
# kinds of timing evidence: ["publisher's stated time", 'shadows', 'timestamped posts']
# consistent with one trip along the road: True
blocks.caption: A consistency check of the reported sightings: times only move forward and places only move along the road. Three different kinds of timing evidence agree, which is what makes the timeline strong.

blocks.md:
**How it held up.** On 24 May 2018 the Joint Investigation Team (JIT, the Dutch-led criminal investigation) announced it was convinced the launcher "originates from the 53rd Anti Aircraft Missile brigade", based in Kursk, after finding a combination of features that "can be considered as a fingerprint" on only one launcher, which had travelled in that brigade's convoy from 23 to 25 June 2014.

On 17 November 2022 the District Court of The Hague convicted three defendants of causing the crash and of the murder of all 298 people on board, and acquitted a fourth. The court found the launcher had been moved from Donetsk through Makiivka, Zuhres and Torez to Snizhne and on towards Pervomaiskyi, supported by footage and telephone mast data. Of photos of the missile's smoke trail taken from a balcony in Torez, it said "Nothing indicates any tampering"; of the images of the launcher, that they had been "verified to the extent possible with regard to location and timing".

blocks.title: From social media posts to a verdict (years after January 2014)

scenes.caption: July 2014: the shootdown, and within days the first public photos and videos of the launcher.

November 2014: Bellingcat's report geolocates and chronolocates the route and links the launcher to the June convoy. July 2016: its two-year update finds Russia's published satellite images were manipulated.
May 2018: the JIT names the 53rd brigade, using a vehicle fingerprint like the one open-source researchers built.
November 2022: the court's verdict, with footage verified for location and timing alongside intercepts and phone data. Open sources were one strand of the evidence, not the whole case.

blocks.md:
**Lessons for practice.**

- **Many weak signals, independently checked, make a strong case.** No single photo proved anything; the route, the times and the vehicle fingerprint together did.
- **State limits.** The 2014 report said plainly where a link "has not been possible to establish", and called one similarity "certainly not in any way conclusive".
- **Verify the other side's evidence too.** Bellingcat's 2016 update reported that satellite images released by the Russian Defence Ministry on 21 July 2014 were "so heavily manipulated that it lacks any credibility as evidence", based on forensic image analysis by the James Martin Center for Non-Proliferation Studies (a research centre at the Middlebury Institute of International Studies at Monterey).
- **Hand over to the formal process.** Courts weighed open sources alongside intercepts, witness testimony and forensic evidence.
MH17 is the model: geolocate each item, chronolocate it with independent methods, fingerprint the object, state the limits, and let formal investigators test it.

blocks.question: What made the 17 July timeline in Bellingcat's report persuasive?
options: Several independent kinds of timing evidence (stated times, shadows, timestamped posts) agreed with one route
A single high-resolution photo
A confession posted online
The number of people who shared the photos
blocks.explain: Independent methods agreeing is what makes a timeline robust. Sharing counts are popularity, not evidence, and no single photo carried the case.

blocks.question: How did the court treat the open-source photos and videos?
options: It excluded them as unreliable social media
It used them as one strand, verified for location and timing and checked for tampering, alongside other evidence
It relied on them alone
It accepted them without any checks
blocks.explain: The judgment describes verifying footage for location and timing, finding no tampering, and weighing it with intercepts and phone data.

lessons.title: Archiving: capturing evidence that will still be trusted later

blocks.md:
Online material disappears: posts are deleted, accounts suspended, pages edited. The Berkeley Protocol warns that without "timely preservation", once-public information can become unavailable. And a screenshot alone is weak evidence, because anyone can edit one. Preservation means capturing material completely and in a way that proves it has not changed since.

Tiny example: Northwind's status page says the VPN is degraded on Tuesday and normal on Wednesday, with no history. If the incident review needs Tuesday's text, only a capture taken on Tuesday, with a recorded time and a hash, can show what it said.

**What the Berkeley Protocol says to capture**, with the first three as "a minimum standard for providing evidence in court":

1. The **target web address** (URL).
2. The page's **HTML source code**, which holds more than the visible page.
3. A **full-page capture** with the date and time.
4. **Embedded media** such as images and videos, as files.
5. **Embedded metadata** and **contextual data** such as comments and upload details, where relevant.
6. **Collection data**: who collected it, from which machine and IP address, with which virtual identity if any, and when, from a clock synchronised with NTP (Network Time Protocol).
7. A **hash value** for each file at the point of collection, using the currently accepted standard; the Protocol points to NIST for guidance.

The course *Incident response and digital forensics* teaches chain of custody; the same idea applies here.

blocks.caption: A capture record for two stand-in files. SHA-256 is used here; anyone can recompute the hashes later and compare.

blocks.title: Capturing a page so the capture can be trusted later

scenes.caption: The analyst fetches the page from a research environment, saving the HTML and a full-page screenshot.
Optionally, an independent public archive also captures it. A third party's copy is harder to dispute.
Files are hashed immediately and stored with the collection record: URL, UTC time, collector, purpose.
Months later a reviewer recomputes the hashes. A match shows the files are unchanged since collection.

blocks.prompt: After collection, someone opens page.html and adds a single space at the end. How different is its new SHA-256 hash?
blocks.reveal: **Completely different.** Running it gave `e8ee6dbf9b0e663b5b74df87cb89ee51a9e6fc2ff4e5e6422b7f82ef5b6319f7` instead of `491c710c...`. That is the point: any change, however small, is detectable, so a matching hash shows nothing changed. The hash cannot show *what* the page said before collection, only that the stored copy has not changed since.

blocks.md: **Tools that do this at scale.** The **WARC** format (Web ARChive, ISO 28500, maintained by the International Internet Preservation Consortium) stores the actual HTTP requests and responses of a crawl as records. Every record must carry a `WARC-Record-ID`, `Content-Length`, `WARC-Date` (UTC) and `WARC-Type`, and may carry digests of its contents:

blocks.code:
WARC/1.1
WARC-Type: warcinfo
WARC-Date: 2006-09-19T17:20:14Z
WARC-Record-ID: <urn:uuid:d7ae5c10-e6b3-4d27-967d-34780c58ba39>
Content-Type: application/warc-fields
Content-Length: 381
blocks.caption: The start of a record, abridged from the WARC 1.1 specification's example. Record types include warcinfo, request, response, resource, metadata and revisit.

blocks.md:
The **Internet Archive's Save Page Now** captures a single page on request and returns a permanent address for the copy; its help page notes it saves the page's images and style sheets but not the pages it links to, and that some sites prohibit crawling. Public archives are good corroboration, but they capture what *their* crawler saw, which may differ from what you saw while logged in or in another country.

**Do not archive what you should not keep.** Data minimisation still applies: archive the post that answers the requirement, not a whole profile of a bystander.
Capture URL, source, full-page image and media; record who, when (UTC, synced clock) and why; hash every file at collection; keep a read-only copy.

blocks.question: Which item is not part of the Berkeley Protocol's minimum standard for court evidence?
options: The URL
The HTML source code
A full-page capture with date and time
The investigator's personal opinion of the poster
blocks.explain: The minimum three are URL, HTML source and a full-page capture. Opinions belong in analysis, clearly labelled, not in the capture.

blocks.question: What does a matching SHA-256 hash, recomputed months later, prove?
options: That the web page was truthful
That the page never changed online
That the stored file is unchanged since its hash was recorded
Who wrote the page
blocks.explain: A hash proves integrity of the stored copy from the moment it was hashed. Truth, authorship and the live page's history need other evidence.

lessons.title: Bulk collection and its ethics: the Parler archive (2021)

blocks.md:
Sometimes a whole platform's public content can be copied. Doing so raises two separate questions: a **security** question for the platform (why was that so easy?) and an **ethics** question for the collector (should all of it be kept, by whom, for what?).

Tiny example: a forum numbers its posts 1, 2, 3 in the web address. Anyone who sees post 5000 can guess that 4999 and 5001 exist, and a script can walk through every number.

**What happened.** In January 2021, after the 6 January attack on the US Capitol, Amazon Web Services cut off hosting for Parler, a social network that had been used to plan and coordinate the mob. In the days and hours before the shutdown, a group led by a pseudonymous hacker using the handle @donk_enby archived what Wired (12 January 2021) called "dozens of terabytes" of Parler data to the Internet Archive; @donk_enby said it was about 99 percent of the site's public content.

Wired's account of why it was easy: Parler ordered posts by number in its URLs, "Increase a value in a Parler post url by one, and you'd get the next post"; it did not require authentication to view public posts; and it had no **rate limiting** (a cap on how many requests one client may make in a period). Kenneth White, co-director of the Open Crypto Audit Project, called it an **insecure direct object reference** (IDOR). Parler also had not stripped geolocation metadata from images and videos.

**Precisely what the bug was.** OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) defines IDOR as accessing objects "by manipulating identifiers" because of a missing per-object authorisation check. Parler's posts were meant to be public, so the core failure was **enumerability**: predictable IDs plus no limits let anyone copy everything, not only what they were shown. @donk_enby said "Only things that were available publicly via the web were archived"; Wired reported rumours of an administrator-level hack were false.

blocks.code:
# VULNERABLE: public posts stored under counting IDs, no limits
posts, next_id = {}, 1000

def publish(text, media_meta):
    global next_id
    next_id += 1
    posts[next_id] = {"text": text, "meta": media_meta}  # GPS kept
    return next_id

def get_post(post_id, client):
    return posts.get(post_id)          # anyone, any rate

for i in range(5):
    publish(f"post {i}", {"gps": (12.34, 56.78)})

# A crawler only needs one ID to find all the others
found = [get_post(i, "crawler") for i in range(1001, 1006)]
print(len([p for p in found if p]), "posts fetched;", found[0]["meta"])

# Output:
# 5 posts fetched; {'gps': (12.34, 56.78)}
blocks.caption: Vulnerable pattern: counting IDs, no limits, metadata kept. The crawler walks the numbers and gets every post with its location.

Fixed: random 128-bit IDs cannot be guessed, a token bucket allows a burst of 10 and then 1 request per second per client, and an allowlist keeps only safe metadata. After the burst, 91 of 100 rapid guesses are refused.

blocks.md:
**Why each fix works, and its limit.**

- **Random IDs** make walking the ID space hopeless: $2^{128}$ possibilities. OWASP calls them defence in depth only: private objects still need an authorisation check on every request.
- **Rate limiting** turns "copy the site in a night" into "copy it over years", and makes bulk crawling visible. Determined crawlers spread across many addresses, so limits should be paired with detection.
- **Metadata allowlisting** means that even content that is copied carries no location.

**Detect**: alert on clients requesting many distinct objects in sequence, and on traffic to IDs that were never linked anywhere. **Respond**: block or slow the client, and review what was exposed in the meantime.

blocks.title: Enumeration before and after the fixes

scenes.caption: Vulnerable: the crawler asks for post 1001 and gets it, with GPS.
It simply adds one. Every number returns a post; nothing slows it down.
Fixed: a guessed ID matches nothing, because real IDs are random.
After a burst of 10 requests, the token bucket refuses the rest, and the burst itself is a detection signal for the platform's security team.

blocks.md:
**The ethics question.** Public archives of the Parler data let journalists and researchers study the attack; Gizmodo used video GPS data to map posts near the Capitol. The same archive also held, as Wired put it, content likely "revealing the GPS coordinates of many of their homes", for users who had nothing to do with the riot. The Berkeley Protocol's data minimisation principle (collect what is justified, necessary and proportional) and its legality principle (persistent monitoring and "systematic collection and long-term retention of personal data" may need extra safeguards) both apply.

For your own work: bulk collection needs a stronger justification, a stated retention limit, access controls, and a plan for the bystanders' data it inevitably includes.
Predictable IDs, no rate limits and unstripped metadata let a platform be copied wholesale. Defenders fix all three; collectors still owe the people in the data minimisation and care.

blocks.question: Parler's posts were public. Why was the design still a security failure?
options: Public posts should never be visible to anyone
Predictable IDs and no rate limits let anyone copy everything, including location metadata, in bulk
The posts were encrypted badly
The two-factor authentication gave administrators away
blocks.explain: The issue was enumerability at scale plus metadata. Wired reported the administrator-hack rumour was false; public visibility of individual posts was intended.

blocks.question: After switching to random IDs, what does OWASP say is still required for private objects?
options: An authorisation check on every object access
Nothing: random IDs are sufficient
Longer URLs
Moving to a different cloud provider
blocks.explain: OWASP's IDOR guidance treats unguessable IDs as defence in depth; access control must still be checked per object, since URLs leak.

lessons.title: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint

blocks.md:
Many OSINT courses spend days on finding people. This one deliberately does not, because the same steps that let an investigator trace a fraudster let a stalker trace a victim, and the course has no way to know who is reading. What every security professional does need is to understand the **people-data industry**, the law around it, and how to shrink their own and their colleagues' exposure. The courses *Privacy engineering* and *Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher* go deeper.

Tiny example: a staff member at Northwind's help desk is targeted by a caller who knows their home town and their manager's name. Nothing was hacked; both facts came from a broker profile and a public professional profile.

**Data brokers.** California law defines a data broker as a business that knowingly collects and sells to third parties the personal information of a consumer "with whom the business does not have a direct relationship". People-search sites are the consumer face of this industry: they assemble public records and purchased data into profiles.

California's **Delete Act** (SB 362) created **DROP**, the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, run by the California Privacy Protection Agency. It opened to California residents in January 2026 and lets one request reach every registered broker; from 1 August 2026 brokers must access it "at least once every 45 days" and process deletion requests. In the EU and UK, the GDPR's rights of access and erasure apply to brokers as to anyone else.

**Why this matters to security teams.** Broker profiles, breach data and public professional profiles are the raw material of social engineering: help-desk impersonation, SIM swaps (talking a mobile carrier into moving someone's phone number to an attacker's SIM card) and targeted phishing (see *Social engineering, human factors and physical security* and *Phishing, social engineering and email security*). Executive protection programmes therefore review what is public about senior staff, **with their agreement**, and help them remove it. That is the defensible form of people-focused OSINT: about yourself or a consenting colleague, aimed at reducing exposure.

**Checking breach exposure without exposing yourself.** Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), a breach notification service run by Troy Hunt, offers a Pwned Passwords API that uses **k-anonymity** (you hide among at least k others who look the same), a model proposed by Junade Ali at Cloudflare and [launched in February 2018](https://www.troyhunt.com/ive-just-launched-pwned-passwords-version-2/). Your client sends only the first 5 hex characters of the password's SHA-1 hash (an older hash function with a 40-hex-character output); the service returns every hash suffix starting with them, and the comparison happens on your machine. The `Add-Padding` header pads the reply so its size reveals nothing either.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, urllib.request

def times_seen(password):
    digest = hashlib.sha1(password.encode()).hexdigest().upper()
    prefix, suffix = digest[:5], digest[5:]
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/{prefix}",
        headers={"Add-Padding": "true", "User-Agent": "course-demo"})
    lines = urllib.request.urlopen(req).read().decode().splitlines()
    print(f"sent {prefix}, got {len(lines)} suffixes back")
    for line in lines:
        s, count = line.split(":")
        if s == suffix:
            return int(count)
    return 0

print("P@ssw0rd seen", times_seen("P@ssw0rd"), "times")

# Output (November 2026; counts grow over time and padding is random):
# sent 21BD1, got 1999 suffixes back
# P@ssw0rd seen 6421554 times
blocks.caption: Checks a well-known bad password from Troy Hunt's own example. The service learns only 21BD1, which thousands of different passwords share.

blocks.title: A k-anonymity range query

scenes.caption: The client hashes the password locally: SHA-1 of P@ssw0rd is 21BD12DC183F740EE76F27B78EB39C8AD972A757.
Only the 5-character prefix leaves the machine.
The service returns every suffix with that prefix, with counts, padded with fake entries.
The client finds its own suffix in the list. The service never learns which line, or whether any line, was the match.

blocks.md:
**Shrinking your own footprint**, a checklist to run on yourself:

- Search your name, usernames and email addresses logged out, in more than one engine, and list what appears.
- Review privacy settings on every social and professional profile; remove home town, birthday and family details from public view.
- Strip location from photos before posting (lesson 7) and post travel afterwards, not during.
- Use separate email addresses for public, work and account-recovery purposes; turn on MFA (multi-factor authentication) everywhere, preferring passkeys (sign-in keys stored on your device that replace passwords and resist phishing).
- Check your own addresses in HIBP and change any reused password.
- Request removal from people-search sites and brokers, through DROP if you live in California or GDPR erasure requests in the EU and UK.

The EFF's (Electronic Frontier Foundation) [Surveillance Self-Defense](https://ssd.eff.org/) guides cover more.

Check only your own accounts, or colleagues' with their consent. Looking up someone else's email in breach data or a broker profile, without a lawful basis, is exactly the profiling this course rules out.
Understand the people-data industry so you can defend against it: brokers sell profiles, attackers use them, and you shrink exposure with settings, separation, MFA and removal requests.

blocks.question: What does the Pwned Passwords service learn when you check a password with the range API?
options: The full password
The full SHA-1 hash
Only a 5-character hash prefix shared by many passwords
Your email address
blocks.explain: Only the prefix is sent; matching happens locally, and padding hides the response size. That is the k-anonymity design.

blocks.question: Which is the defensible form of people-focused OSINT for a security team?
options: Profiling customers who complain online
Finding home addresses of a competitor's staff
Checking breach data for any email address you are curious about
Reviewing what is public about consenting staff, then helping them remove it
blocks.explain: Consent plus a protective purpose makes it legitimate. The other options profile people without a lawful basis or their agreement.

lessons.title: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise

blocks.md:
This lesson runs one engagement end to end: an OSINT review of Northwind's own exposure, requested by its security lead. Every step uses a lesson from this course.

Tiny example of the output: "An internal VPN setup guide is indexed by search engines at docs.northwind.example/vpn-guide.pdf (capture record CR-0007, 20 Nov 2026 10:02 UTC, SHA-256 in the record). Severity high. Fix: remove and protect the file, request de-indexing. Owner: IT operations. Due: 48 hours." One fact, its evidence, why it matters and what to do.

**The engagement, step by step.**

1. **Authorise and plan** (lessons 2 and 3): written requirements from the security lead, a collection plan with legal basis and retention, stop conditions for personal data.
2. **Prepare the environment** (lesson 4): a separate research profile; queries logged.
3. **Collect** (lessons 5 to 7): search operators on own domains, RDAP and certificate logs, code hosts, metadata of published files.
4. **Preserve** (lesson 12): URL, source, capture, hashes, collection record.
5. **Verify** (lessons 8 to 10): is each finding real, current and correctly attributed? Is the host really Northwind's?
6. **Analyse and report**: findings ranked by severity, each with evidence, owner and fix, and a section on what could not be checked.
7. **Remediate and re-check**: the same queries a month later should return nothing.

blocks.title: A two-week own-organisation OSINT review

scenes.caption: Days 0 to 2: authorisation and the collection plan come first. Nothing is collected before they are signed.
Days 2 to 7: collection and preservation run together; each capture is hashed as it is taken.
Days 5 to 9: verification overlaps the end of collection; false positives (someone else's host, an old file) are removed.
Days 9 to 14: report, fixes by owners, then a re-check with the same queries. Retention ends: working copies are deleted as the plan said.

blocks.code:
# Turn raw observations from an own-organisation OSINT review into findings
observations = [
    ("CT log", "jira-test.northwind.example", "unknown host, no owner"),
    ("search", "docs.northwind.example/vpn-guide.pdf", "internal guide indexed"),
    ("photo metadata", "press-kit/team.jpg", "GPS in staff photos"),
    ("code host", "public repo northwind/tools", "API key in history"),
    ("RDAP", "northwind.example", "expires in 40 days"),
]
RULES = [("API key", "high", "rotate key, then purge history"),
         ("internal guide", "high", "remove, request de-indexing"),
         ("unknown host", "medium", "find owner or shut down"),
         ("expires", "medium", "renew, enable auto-renew"),
         ("GPS", "low", "strip metadata in publishing workflow")]
ORDER = {"high": 0, "medium": 1, "low": 2}

findings = []
for source, where, what in observations:
    sev, fix = next((s, f) for key, s, f in RULES if key in what)
    findings.append((sev, where, what, fix))
for sev, where, what, fix in sorted(findings, key=lambda f: ORDER[f[0]]):
    print(f"{sev:6s} {where:38s} {fix}")

# Output:
# high   docs.northwind.example/vpn-guide.pdf   remove, request de-indexing
# high   public repo northwind/tools            rotate key, then purge history
# medium jira-test.northwind.example            find owner or shut down
# medium northwind.example                      renew, enable auto-renew
# low    press-kit/team.jpg                     strip metadata in publishing workflow
blocks.caption: Turning observations into a ranked findings list. In a real report each line also links to its capture record and hash.

blocks.md:
**Writing it up.** Follow the Berkeley Protocol's accuracy principle: "Analytical conclusions should not be exaggerated or overstated", in "clear, objective, fact-based language". Separate what you observed from what you infer. Say what you could not verify. Keep personal data out of the report unless the finding requires it; describe an exposed staff list rather than reproducing it. The course *Writing and influence for security work* covers making reports people act on.

**Where this leads.** OSINT skills feed threat intelligence, penetration testing, investigations and journalism. The SANS Institute, a security training company, offers a dedicated course, [SEC497 *Practical Open-Source Intelligence*](https://www.sans.org/cyber-security-courses/practical-open-source-intelligence/), whose syllabus spans OPSEC, search, metadata, geolocation, infrastructure research and a capture-the-flag exercise for a fictional client.

**Where to practise legally and ethically**:

- Bellingcat's [beginner's guide to geolocating videos](https://www.bellingcat.com/resources/how-tos/2014/07/09/a-beginners-guide-to-geolocation/) (lesson 9): the method worked step by step on a public place, ready to repeat on landmarks.
- [GeoGuessr](https://www.geoguessr.com/): a game that drops you at a street-level location to identify; good geolocation practice on public places.
- The [Berkeley Protocol](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/2024-01/OHCHR_BerkeleyProtocol.pdf) itself, including its investigation plan and data collection templates.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (formerly picoCTF) and [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/): practice challenges and defensive investigations built for learners.
- Your own organisation, with written permission: the most useful target of all.
Never practise on real private people, including friends who "don't mind". Use public landmarks, fictional scenarios, practice platforms, and your own organisation with written permission.
An ethical OSINT engagement is authorised, planned, minimal, preserved, verified and reported with its limits, and it ends with fixes and deleted working data.

blocks.question: Your report includes a finding that a public spreadsheet lists staff home addresses. How should the report present it?
options: Describe the exposure, location of the file and fix, without reproducing the addresses
Paste the spreadsheet into an appendix for completeness
Leave it out, since it is not about systems
List the addresses of senior staff only
blocks.explain: The finding is the exposure; reproducing personal data spreads it further. It is in scope because it enables social engineering against the organisation.

blocks.question: One month after fixes, the same queries still find the VPN guide in search results. What does that most likely show?
options: The original finding was wrong
The fix is incomplete: the file or a cached copy is still reachable, so remediation continues
Search engines are unreliable, so the result can be ignored
The re-check step is unnecessary
blocks.explain: A re-check exists to catch exactly this: a file left in another location, a mirror, or a cache not yet removed. The finding stays open until the re-check is clean.
